notes.subject: plate
notes.text: Long white plates with the blue EU strip on the left; Swiss plates are long and white but have no strip.

notes.subject: bollard
notes.text: White bollards with a black top, often with a small nipple-shaped cap, and a dark red or dark grey reflector.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Pedestrian crossing signs show two horizontal dashed lines instead of zebra stripes; every neighbour uses stripes.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: One-way signs say just EINBAHN, unique to this country.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Blue road markers with white numbers and one decimal after a comma are very recognisable.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Direction and town-entrance signs are white with a blue outline and a unique font; the northern neighbour uses yellow town signs.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Bus stop signs show a yellow and green circle with an H.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Chevrons come in white on red and red on yellow.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: No stopping and no waiting signs often carry the words Anfang or Ende (start or end).

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Simple dead-end signs show a white upside-down T, mostly unique here.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Road signs are sometimes fixed with four metal clips, unusual in central Europe.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Round wooden poles are the most common pole type.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Yellow natural gas marker poles resembling snow poles are unique here.

notes.subject: language
notes.text: Letters Ä, Ö, Ü and ß are used; the same language is spoken in the northern neighbour and Switzerland.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Only generation 3 and 4 coverage plus smallcam; Switzerland is always low-cam with a big blur, and the northern neighbour is generation 4 only.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Mostly mountainous and forested; the east and northeast are flatter farmland, though still hilly.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Alpine houses with light walls, wooden balconies or panelling on the top floor, and wide dark wooden roofs.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Neon-yellow bus stop poles and yellow-white striped poles and signposts appear in the far west.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: White kilometre markers appear in the far west and on one road in western Salzburg.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Green Güterweg signs are found in the east; white ones with a black outline are mainly in the north.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Signs with yellow and blue borders, matching the regional flag, occur in the northeast.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Vineyards are limited to the far east, around the capital and the big steppe lake.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: A tin-foil style antenna on the camera car appears in the west, mostly near the Swiss border.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: The capital has dark blue street plaques with a white serif font, starting with the district number.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Poles in the capital and Innsbruck carry red-and-white tape like the flag; the capital's tapes are thinner, usually two per pole.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: A vast lake on the western border, far larger than any other lake in the mountains.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Road numbers generally increase from east to west; B-roads 222-230 are the exception, inside the capital.
